title: Keeping the needs of woman and baby together
blurb: Plan care for the woman and her newborn as one unit, avoid needless separation, and keep them connected when they must be apart.
question: Sophie has a caesarean under general anaesthetic and goes to recovery while her healthy baby, Leo, stays with her partner. How should the midwife keep Sophie's and Leo's needs together?

teach.body: Formally, midwives must ensure that the needs of women and newborn infants are considered together as a priority in all settings, even when they have to be cared for separately (SPM 2.6). In plain English: the woman and her baby are a pair. Plan for both at once, avoid separating them for routine tasks, and when illness forces them apart, keep the link alive through information, milk and contact.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives 2.6

teach.h: The first hour after birth (NICE NG235)

items.label: Dry, cover with a warm blanket, airway supported

teach.caption: NG235 1.11.10: avoid separation in the first hour for routine weighing, measuring or bathing unless she asks or the baby needs immediate care.

teach.h: When she is not well enough
teach.body: If the woman is not well enough for skin-to-skin, encourage her birth companion to have skin-to-skin contact instead (NG235 1.11.7). Keep the baby warm and dry, and prioritise optimal airway positioning with the head supported, explaining to the woman and companion how to maintain the airway (1.11.8, 1.11.9). Bring the baby to her as soon as she is able.

root.label: Woman or baby needs extra care

head: Situation
Joint-care action
rows: Assess the baby for infection too (NG194 1.2.8)
Breaks of up to 30 minutes for breastfeeding (CG98)
Mother and baby unit if admitted within 12 months (CG192)
Assess both woman and baby first (NG194 1.1.10)

teach.body: While Sophie recovers from the general anaesthetic, midwife Priya supports her partner to hold Leo skin-to-skin, keeping Leo's airway clear. Routine weighing waits. As soon as Sophie is awake and safe, Priya brings Leo to her, helps with skin-to-skin and a first feed, and explains what happened in her absence. Both are observed and recorded as a pair, and they move to the postnatal ward together.

teach.h: When the baby is on the neonatal unit
teach.caption: UNICEF UK Baby Friendly neonatal standards: close and loving relationships, breastmilk and breastfeeding when possible, and valuing parents as partners in care.

teach.text: 'Mother has diabetes' or 'baby needs glucose checks' is not a reason to admit a well baby to the neonatal unit. NG3 1.5.2: babies of women with diabetes stay with their mothers unless complications or abnormal clinical signs need special or intensive care.

items.label: after birth: mother and baby unit for admission

items: SPM 2.6: consider the woman's and baby's needs together, even when cared for apart.
Skin-to-skin as soon as possible; companion skin-to-skin if she is unwell; airway supported.
No routine separation in the first hour; weigh and measure after it.
If the woman transfers after birth, the baby goes with her; babies of women with diabetes stay with her unless unwell.
When apart: updates, expressing, visits, and a mother and baby unit for severe mental illness.

summary: You can now plan care for a woman and her newborn as one unit, from skin-to-skin and the first hour to transfers and illness. You can also keep them connected when separation cannot be avoided.

A.q: A healthy term baby is in skin-to-skin contact with his mother 10 minutes after birth. When should the midwife weigh him?
options: Soon after the first hour, keeping them together until then
Straight away, before skin-to-skin contact continues
Within 15 minutes of birth for the birth register
After his first bath on the postnatal ward
A.why: NG235 1.11.10 and 1.11.14: avoid separation in the first hour for routine procedures; record birth weight soon after the first hour.

whyNot.1: Interrupting skin-to-skin for weighing is the routine separation NICE advises against.
whyNot.2: There is no 15-minute requirement; weighing waits until after the first hour.
whyNot.3: Bathing is also a routine procedure, and weight is recorded soon after the first hour.

A.q: After a major haemorrhage, Ines is too unwell for skin-to-skin contact with her baby. What should the midwife offer?
options: Place the baby in a warmed cot until Ines recovers
Transfer the baby to the neonatal unit for warmth
Wrap the baby and ask a maternity support worker to hold him
Skin-to-skin contact with her birth companion instead
A.why: NG235 1.11.7: if the woman is not well enough, encourage her birth companion to have skin-to-skin contact instead.

whyNot.0: A cot loses the benefits of skin-to-skin when a companion can provide it.
whyNot.1: A well baby does not need neonatal admission for warmth.
whyNot.2: Staff holding the baby is not the NICE recommendation when a companion is present.

A.q: After a home birth, Dana needs transfer to the obstetric unit for a retained placenta. Her baby is well. What should happen to the baby?
options: The baby stays at home with Dana's partner
The baby goes to the neonatal unit to be observed
The baby travels with Dana to the obstetric unit
The baby follows later with another family member
A.why: NG235 1.5.6: if a woman is transferred to an obstetric unit after the birth, ensure that her baby goes with her.

whyNot.0: Leaving the baby behind separates the pair without clinical reason.
whyNot.1: A well baby does not need neonatal admission.
whyNot.3: Delayed transfer of the baby separates them unnecessarily.

B.q: Fatima has gestational diabetes treated with insulin. Her baby is born at 39 weeks, well, and needs blood glucose monitoring. Where should the baby be cared for?
options: On the neonatal unit for glucose monitoring
In the ward nursery for the first 24 hours
On the neonatal unit until feeding is established
With his mother, unless complications arise
B.why: NG3 1.5.2: babies of women with diabetes should stay with their mothers unless complications or abnormal clinical signs mean admission to intensive or special care.

whyNot.0: Glucose monitoring can be done with the baby beside his mother.
whyNot.1: Nursery care separates a well baby from his mother without need.
whyNot.2: Feeding is best established with the baby kept with his mother.

B.q: On day 4, Grace has a fever and offensive lochia; puerperal sepsis is suspected. Her baby is breastfeeding. What should the midwife do for the baby?
options: Assess the baby for signs of infection
Separate the baby to prevent cross-infection
Stop breastfeeding until her antibiotics finish
Refer the baby's care to the health visitor
B.why: NG194 1.2.8: if the woman has confirmed or suspected puerperal sepsis, assess the baby for symptoms or signs of infection.

whyNot.1: Separation is not recommended; the baby needs assessment alongside his mother.
whyNot.2: Stopping breastfeeding is not advised and harms feeding.
whyNot.3: The baby needs prompt assessment now by the maternity team.

B.q: A breastfed baby on the postnatal ward needs phototherapy for jaundice. His mother asks if she can still feed him. What should the midwife advise?
options: Give formula in the cot so treatment is not paused
Wait to breastfeed until phototherapy has stopped
Feed him in short breaks of up to 30 minutes
Express milk, as no breaks are allowed in treatment
B.why: CG98: during phototherapy, give short breaks of up to 30 minutes for breastfeeding, and do not give extra fluids to breastfed babies routinely.

whyNot.0: Routine formula or extra fluids are not recommended for breastfed babies on phototherapy.
whyNot.1: Stopping breastfeeding for the whole treatment is unnecessary.

C.q: Three weeks after birth, Amy develops postpartum psychosis and needs inpatient care. Her baby is well. What does NICE CG192 recommend?
options: Admission to an adult acute ward, with baby at home
Admission to a specialist mother and baby unit
Readmission to the postnatal ward with her baby
Temporary foster care for the baby during treatment
C.why: CG192 1.10.1: women who need inpatient care for a mental health problem within 12 months of childbirth should normally be admitted to a specialist mother and baby unit.

whyNot.0: An adult ward separates mother and baby when a mother and baby unit is recommended.
whyNot.2: A postnatal ward cannot provide specialist psychiatric inpatient care.
whyNot.3: Separation is not the default; the mother and baby unit keeps them together safely.

C.q: Baby Noah is on the neonatal unit; his mother Kim is recovering from a caesarean on the postnatal ward. Which plan best keeps their needs together?
options: Focus on Kim's recovery; the neonatal team handles Noah
Pass updates about Noah to Kim through her partner
Wait to start expressing until Kim can walk to the unit
Support Kim to express, update her and help her visit
C.why: SPM 2.6 asks midwives to consider both together even when cared for apart. Baby Friendly neonatal standards: enable breastmilk, close relationships and parents as partners in care.

whyNot.0: Splitting care ignores the shared needs SPM 2.6 protects.
whyNot.1: Kim should receive information directly, as Noah's mother and partner in his care.
whyNot.2: Delaying expressing harms milk supply; support can start on the ward.

C.q: During skin-to-skin contact straight after birth, what should the midwife prioritise and explain to the woman and her birth companion?
options: Keeping the baby uncovered to maximise skin contact
Keeping the baby's head supported so the airway is open
Lying the woman flat on her back throughout contact
Limiting contact to 10 minutes before newborn checks
C.why: NG235 1.11.9: prioritise optimal airway positioning, supporting the head so the airway does not become obstructed, and explain how to maintain it.

whyNot.0: NG235 1.11.8: cover the baby with a warm, dry blanket while maintaining skin-to-skin.
whyNot.2: Positioning is about the baby's airway; lying flat is not recommended.
whyNot.3: Avoid separation for routine checks in the first hour.

reteach.title: Think 'dyad', not two patients
reteach.question: When you care for a woman, who else is in the room, even if he is on another ward?

blocks.body: Every plan for the woman should ask 'what does this mean for her baby?', and every plan for the baby should ask 'what does this mean for his mother?'. Keep them together whenever it is safe: skin-to-skin, transfers together, babies of mothers with diabetes beside them, mother and baby units. When apart, build bridges with updates, milk and visits.

blocks.text: A routine task is not a reason to separate a well mother and baby in the first hour, unless the woman asks for it.

explain.body: Skin-to-skin as soon as possible (NG235 1.11.7), warm and dry with airway supported (1.11.8, 1.11.9), no separation for routine procedures (1.11.10), breastfeeding ideally within 1 hour (1.11.11), weight and head circumference soon after the first hour (1.11.14).

test.q: A woman asks for her baby to be weighed straight away so she can tell her family. What is the correct approach?
options: Weigh the baby, as she has requested it
Refuse, as weighing must wait an hour
Ask the partner to decide for her
Delay until the baby's first bath
test.why: NG235 1.11.10: avoid separation for routine procedures unless these are requested by the woman. Her informed request should be respected.

whyNot.1: The first-hour guidance allows procedures the woman requests.
whyNot.2: The decision is the woman's, not her partner's.
whyNot.3: This ignores her request and adds another separation.

explain.body: If the woman transfers to an obstetric unit after birth, the baby goes with her (NG235 1.5.6). Babies of women with diabetes stay with their mothers unless complications need special or intensive care (NG3 1.5.2). Before transfer home, assess both (NG194 1.1.10).

test.q: Which statement about babies of women with diabetes is correct according to NICE NG3?
options: They are admitted to special care for the first 24 hours
They are bottle fed until their glucose is stable
They stay with their mothers unless complications arise
They are cared for in the ward nursery overnight
test.why: NG3 1.5.2: babies of women with diabetes should stay with their mothers unless complications or abnormal clinical signs need intensive or special care.

whyNot.0: Routine admission is not recommended for a well baby.
whyNot.1: NG3 advises early feeding, not routine bottle feeding.
whyNot.3: Nursery care separates a well baby without need.

explain.body: When the baby needs neonatal care, keep the woman informed, support expressing and breastmilk, enable visits and skin-to-skin when possible. Baby Friendly neonatal standards value parents as partners in care.

test.q: According to UNICEF UK Baby Friendly neonatal standards, how should parents of babies on the neonatal unit be regarded?
options: As visitors to the neonatal unit
As partners in their baby's care
As observers until discharge home
As decision makers for staff rotas
test.why: The Baby Friendly neonatal standards include valuing parents as partners in care.

whyNot.0: Treating parents as visitors limits their role.
whyNot.2: Parents are involved in care, not just observers.
whyNot.3: Staffing is not a parental role.

explain.body: Suspected puerperal sepsis: assess the baby for infection (NG194 1.2.8). Phototherapy: breaks of up to 30 minutes for breastfeeding (CG98). Inpatient mental health care within 12 months of birth: specialist mother and baby unit (CG192 1.10.1).

test.q: A woman needs psychiatric inpatient care 6 months after birth. Which setting does NICE CG192 recommend?
options: A general adult psychiatric ward
A postnatal ward side room
A crisis house without her baby
A specialist mother and baby unit
test.why: CG192 1.10.1: for inpatient mental health care within 12 months of childbirth, admit to a specialist mother and baby unit.

whyNot.0: A general ward separates her from her baby.
whyNot.1: A postnatal ward is not a specialist psychiatric setting.
whyNot.2: This separates mother and baby without need.
